scope: Africa; circa 1100-1400 rural systems, irrigation landscapes, archaeological settlement controls, and explicitly rejected broad demography

records.label: Fayyum villages cadastral and irrigation register
pressure_evidence: al-Nabulusi surveyed village-by-village agricultural conditions, taxes, water rights, and irrigation officials in 1245
the register treats the village as the basic unit of agricultural and social reproduction
Fayyum arable area depended on canal allocations and Lake Qarun water level
shock_flags: fiscal record is not a population census
records.food_regime: basin irrigation, cereals, legumes, livestock, pasture fees, and fish
records.mapped_boundary: Mid-thirteenth-century Fayyum province and its villages; the single EU5 Fayyum location is only a screening proxy

sources.title: Rural Society in Medieval Islam: The Villages of the Fayyum
sources.supports: 1245 village-level taxes, land, water rights, irrigation and agricultural conditions

sources.title: Rural Economy and Tribal Society in Islamic Egypt
sources.supports: quantitative and spatial interpretation of the register

records.notes: This is a high-value rural source but has no defensible headcount in the packet. It should test irrigation, local food, and land-allocation mechanisms only.

records.label: Nile Valley and Delta cadastre population reconstruction

population_interval.semantics: fiscal cadastre-to-population reconstruction; not a saturation interval

pressure_evidence: 1298 and 1315 cadastres report approximately 3,637,000 feddans of assessed land
Nile flood irrigation creates a measurable agricultural denominator
Fayyum and rural Nile registers show local crop and water administration
shock_flags: plague onset near the end of the interval
records.food_regime: Nile flood irrigation, cereals, legumes, livestock, fish, and urban redistribution
records.mapped_boundary: Historical Nile settlement corridor and assessed land; `region=egypt_region` is an approximate EU5 envelope

sources.title: UN Population Bulletin 31-32
sources.supports: 1298/1315 cadastre land totals and population reconstruction

records.notes: This is a documentary validation interval, not a scale anchor. Urban redistribution, fiscal under-registration, and shock timing prevent a saturation inference.

records.label: Broad Mamluk Nile population observation (rejected)
records.food_regime: basin irrigation, cereals, legumes, livestock, fish, and urban redistribution
records.mapped_boundary: Nile settlement corridor is not equivalent to the EU5 Egypt region

sources.title: Mamluk Egypt fiscal and demographic source discussion
sources.supports: shock and boundary confounding reasons for exclusion

records.notes: Kept as an explicit rejected candidate so a broad Egypt number cannot silently re-enter training.

records.label: Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape lower-bound population

population_interval.semantics: explicit one-sided lower bound; no central estimate is asserted

pressure_evidence: SANParks states that the cultural landscape sustained at least 9,000 people at its AD 1220-1300 height
settlements used sorghum, millet, beans, cowpeas, livestock, game, and river fish
river confluence and cultivated floodplain supported a dense state landscape
shock_flags: cultural-landscape boundary differs from game polygon
lower-bound statement rather than saturation estimate
landscape abandoned after the fourteenth century
records.food_regime: sorghum and millet, beans/cowpeas, livestock, game, river fisheries, and long-distance trade
records.mapped_boundary: Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape, approximated by one EU5 Mapungubwe location

sources.title: SANParks Mapungubwe Natural and Cultural History
sources.supports: at least 9,000 people, dates, crops, livestock, game, and fish

sources.title: Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.supports: dependent settlement landscape, state/trade context, and abandonment

records.notes: A strong one-sided historical check but not an intrinsic capacity label: the cultural landscape and game location do not share a verified polygon, and the kingdom was trade-linked.

records.label: Jenné-jeno and Middle Niger settlement system
pressure_evidence: Jenné-jeno exceeded 33 hectares at its apogee and nearby settlements formed a dense cluster
regional surveys report rural settlement density far above modern hinterland density
wetland African rice, millet, sorghum, fishing, livestock, and floodplain specialization supported settlement growth
records.food_regime: African rice, millet, sorghum, livestock, fishing, and floodplain foods
records.mapped_boundary: Middle Niger settlement cluster and rural hinterland; the one-location EU5 proxy is incomplete

sources.title: The Inland Niger Delta before the Empire of Mali
sources.supports: settlement size and dense rural settlement evidence

sources.title: Excavations at Jenné-jeno, Hambarketolo, and Kaniana

records.notes: Do not create a population interval from site hectares. Retain as a qualitative physical-system and settlement-density validation case only.

records.label: Great Zimbabwe archaeological site population constraint

population_interval.semantics: archaeological site-phase interval; explicitly not surrounding-land capacity

pressure_evidence: archaeological spatial models estimate a few thousand coeval residents and reject an unqualified 20,000-person site peak
shock_flags: site population is not surrounding-land capacity
records.food_regime: sorghum and millet, livestock, wild foods, and regional trade
records.mapped_boundary: Great Zimbabwe archaeological site; the game location is much broader

sources.title: The population of Great Zimbabwe
sources.supports: phase-specific site population estimates and rejection of an unqualified 20,000 peak

records.notes: Keep as a negative control for urban/site overinterpretation. Never use this interval to supervise the surrounding EU5 location capacity.

records.label: Lalibela and Lasta medieval agricultural landscape
pressure_evidence: archaeological and archaeobotanical work documents medieval farming communities around Lalibela and Lasta
highland crop and livestock systems used terracing and local water management
landscape surveys show a capital and surrounding rural production, but not a population total
records.food_regime: highland cereals, pulses, livestock, terracing, and localized water management
records.mapped_boundary: Lalibela/Lasta archaeological landscape approximated by location_tag=lalibela

sources.title: On the Agricultural Economy of the Medieval Inhabitants of Lalibela and Environs
sources.supports: medieval crops, livestock, and agricultural economy

sources.title: The Lalibela Rock Hewn Site and its Landscape

records.notes: Do not infer a population interval from church construction or site importance. Use only to test highland crop, terrace, and water-management mechanisms.

records.label: Medieval West African trade-center screening set
records.food_regime: Sahelian millet, sorghum, rice, livestock, fish, and imported trade goods
records.mapped_boundary: Timbuktu, Gao, and Kano urban/trade nodes; no stable rural hinterland boundary

sources.title: West African Regional Development
sources.supports: varied regional adaptations and absence of absolute population data

records.notes: Explicitly rejected for training. Wealth, market reach, or city size cannot label local Malthusian capacity without a rural boundary and pressure evidence.

records.label: Broad premodern African population estimates
records.food_regime: multiple cereal, root-crop, pastoral, fishing, and forest food systems
records.mapped_boundary: Continental aggregate has no capacity-test boundary

sources.title: We do not know the population of every country in the world for the past two thousand years
sources.supports: uncertainty and limitations of broad African totals

records.notes: Continental estimates must remain outside model training and capacity scaling. Africa should instead be evaluated through local physical inputs and vetted local cases.
